title: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The average number of individuals of an animal or plant species depends only indirectly on how many eggs or seeds it produces; high fecundity mainly compensates for heavy destruction, usually early in life.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: So that in all cases, the average number of any animal or plant depends only indirectly on the number of its eggs or seeds.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “Geometrical powers of increase”. Scope: all animals and plants

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.66

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public demographic matrices contain the needed life-history variables for many species, but often not abundance measured on matching populations. Restricted comparative tests are feasible.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Across species, model equilibrium abundance from fecundity and stage-specific mortality, testing whether fecundity effects vanish after early mortality and other vital rates are included. Weak direct effects and compensation by destruction support the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Vital-rate estimates are taxonomically biased.

Matrix databases rarely measure absolute field abundance.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.66
operationalizability: 0.77
data adequacy: 0.49
data existence: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.63

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Fecundity, survival, and at least relative abundance are public for a large comparative sample, and the regression is a standard life-history test. The sample is still a subset of animals and plants, and size confounding is serious though tractable. The statement is close to resolvable for that subset and not yet a full-scope census.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In a phylogenetic regression, predict average abundance from fecundity after controlling for juvenile survival and body size. A weak partial effect of fecundity, together with a positive association between fecundity and early mortality, would support indirect dependence and compensation; a strong direct fecundity-abundance relationship with no early-mortality tradeoff would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Absolute average abundance is missing for many species that have excellent fecundity data.

The joint sample is biased toward well-studied vertebrates, fish, and plants.

Body size drives both fecundity and abundance and must be partialled out.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data existence: 0.74
discriminating power: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.68
